topics.question: How did a prostate-cancer drug's sales incentives influence what doctors prescribed and billed?
topics.documented_conduct: TAP agreed to plead guilty to a conspiracy involving free drug samples; prosecutors also charged individuals with kickback conspiracies. Do not present each individual's charge as a conviction.
topics.health_context: Lupron was used primarily for advanced prostate cancer in men; the story concerns marketing, prescribing incentives and billing, not whether all use of the drug was inappropriate.

source.locator: DOJ release, October 3, 2001, paragraphs describing corporate plea and individual indictment
source.note: Government account of the $875 million resolution, corporate plea and separate allegations against individuals.

angles: What was the free-sample billing mechanism?
How can a grant or trip affect a prescription?
What did the company admit versus what prosecutors alleged?
visual_receipts: Original document headline and highlighted plea terms
Original animated billing flow labeled illustration
topics.limitation: A 2001 case; later individual defendants were reportedly acquitted. Verify court dispositions before naming anyone, and never equate the corporate plea with individual guilt or current practice.

topics.question: Did litigation keep cheaper testosterone gel off the market?
topics.documented_conduct: The Third Circuit affirmed liability for sham patent litigation used to maintain an AndroGel monopoly. A separate reverse-payment claim was reinstated, then withdrawn; do not call that claim a proven violation.
topics.health_context: The product treats certain low-testosterone conditions; a finding about competition does not establish that every testosterone prescription was medically appropriate.

source.locator: FTC release, July 30, 2021, paragraphs on Third Circuit ruling and withdrawn count
source.note: FTC summary distinguishes the surviving liability finding from the withdrawn payment allegation and vacated monetary remedy.

Illustrated timeline of generic market entry
topics.limitation: Distinguish this case from the separate FTC v. Actavis reverse-payment settlement.

topics.question: Why did a supposedly natural male-enhancement product contain prescription ED drugs?
topics.documented_conduct: DOJ described a sentenced seller's coordinated sale of sildenafil-containing products as natural; a separate 2026 FDA lab finding identified undeclared sildenafil and tadalafil in another named product.
topics.health_context: Undeclared ED drugs can interact dangerously with nitrates. The convicted scheme and the later FDA warning involve different products and parties.

source.locator: DOJ sentencing release, March 11, 2019, Silver Bullet marketing and concealment passages
source.note: Court outcome and government account of the all-natural marketing scheme.

additional_sources.locator: FDA warning, May 29, 2026, laboratory finding and nitrate interaction
additional_sources.note: A current example of a separate product with undeclared ED drugs; no inference of common ownership.

angles: What did the label promise versus the laboratory result?
How did the older scheme hide its seller?
Why is an undeclared dose a safety issue?
visual_receipts: FDA product notice with label and finding
topics.limitation: Never infer that every supplement, seller, or online listing is part of the convicted scheme.

topics.question: What was billed during routine testosterone injections at a clinic chain?
topics.documented_conduct: Ageless Men's Health paid $1.6 million to resolve government allegations that it billed Medicare and TRICARE for medically unnecessary office visits during testosterone injections.
topics.health_context: The allegation is about billed evaluation visits; it is not a finding that every injection or testosterone treatment was unnecessary.

source.locator: DOJ release, February 2015, settlement and alleged office-visit billing
source.note: Government settlement announcement; allegations are not adjudicated findings.

angles: What does an injection visit bill actually include?
What did the government allege and what was resolved?
visual_receipts: Original diagram separating injection from office-visit billing
topics.limitation: Settlement does not establish liability; obtain underlying complaint before expanding beyond the release.

topics.question: Did ownership of radiation facilities affect prostate-cancer treatment referrals?
topics.documented_conduct: GAO observed greater IMRT use after some practices began self-referring and concluded financial incentives were likely a major factor. It did not find a covert agreement or establish that each treatment was unnecessary.
topics.health_context: IMRT is a legitimate treatment; the question is how financial interests can affect choices among suitable options.

source.note: Government utilization analysis and its own stated limitations.
